text: Let workshop participants make pieces that go into the installation, and credit them on site.
why: Residents see their own work in public, which builds ownership and brings their families as audience.

text: Keep amplified sound low and pointed away from flats above; end early on weeknights.
why: Void decks sit directly under homes; noise complaints are the quickest way to lose the space.

text: Plan the performance as a small acoustic set, or move it to the nearby open space: Bishan-Toa Payoh TC does not permit variety shows at void decks.
why: The Town Council's booking rates list variety shows as not permitted at void decks but allowed on open spaces.

text: If relying on a licence exemption, keep to its conditions: start after 11am and end by 10.30pm, use at most 4 loudspeakers angled down towards the audience, and do no set-up or teardown between 11pm and 7am.
why: These are the listed conditions for exempt music performances; breaking them means a licence was needed.

text: Keep a step-free route from the nearest lift or bus stop, and put shaded seating near the front for older residents.
why: Neighbourhood audiences include many seniors and families with prams.

text: Keep the site open to everyone during the event — no gated areas or paid zones — if you apply to the Lively Places Fund.
why: The fund requires the space to be accessible to the public at all times and does not support commercial events.

text: Orient the light installation so it reads from the main walkway after dark, and test it at dusk on site.
why: Passers-by become the audience without extra promotion; tropical dusk is short, so timing matters.

text: Have a wet-weather plan: a sheltered fallback spot, covered power points, and a decision time 2 hours before start.
why: Evening thunderstorms are common in Singapore; outdoor electrics and audiences need a clear call.

text: Respond to the street's heritage: keep the five-foot way clear and use the shophouse rhythm (columns, shutters) as the frame rather than covering façades.
why: Keeps pedestrian flow and fits the conservation context that gives the place its identity.

text: Use ground protection under stages and keep cables off tree roots; leave the lawn as found.
why: Park managers judge applications partly on how the site is protected and restored.

text: If the site is in a nature park or on the Rail Corridor and more than 30 people take part, apply for NParks' group activity permit at least 1 month ahead.
why: NParks rejects late applications for organised group activities in those networks.

text: Confirm who manages the site before booking performers or paying deposits.
why: The land owner's consent gates every other permit; this site's owner is not confirmed.

text: Publicise in the languages used in the block (English, Chinese, Malay, Tamil) through the Residents' Network notice boards.
why: Lift-lobby notices reach residents who do not follow social media.

text: Run the drinks stall with a residents' group rather than an outside vendor, and keep cooking off-site.
why: Keeps money in the neighbourhood; some Town Councils prohibit cooking at void decks.

text: Mark a clear entry and exit, keep emergency routes free, and brief volunteers on where to send people if it rains.
why: Small sites fill fast; simple flow planning avoids crowding at pinch points.
